approved: Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would deregulate university fees and extend government-funded places to more types of courses and providers.

Universities and other higher education providers could set their own student contribution amounts, and institutions with 500 or more Commonwealth supported places would have to put 20% of extra revenue into a scholarship scheme for disadvantaged students.
The bill also changes how HELP debts are indexed, introduces a new minimum repayment threshold, removes loan fees and the lifetime fee limit, and ends the HECS-HELP benefit.
Deregulates fees for higher education courses.
Extends demand-driven funding to sub-bachelor qualifications and to private universities and non-university providers.
Requires providers with 500 or more Commonwealth supported places to direct 20% of additional revenue to a Commonwealth Scholarship Scheme.
Introduces new indexation arrangements for HELP debts.
Sets a new minimum repayment threshold for HELP loans.
Removes loan fees and the lifetime fee limit and discontinues the HECS-HELP benefit.
Students, higher education providers (including universities and private providers), and taxpayers.

Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014 - Consideration in Detail - Agree to the bill

Introduced the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, saying it would support an additional 80,000 higher education students a year by 2018, require universities to direct one dollar in every five of additional revenue into a new Commonwealth scholarship scheme for disadvantaged students, and raise the average student contribution to the cost of a degree from 40 per cent to around 50 per cent from January 2016.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, saying higher education funding would grow by over $950 million over four years and more than 80,000 additional students would be supported by 2018, and noted education exports have fallen from about $19 billion in 2009-10 to around $15 billion now.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, saying it cuts approximately $5.8 billion from universities, introduces fees of up to $3,900 for PhDs and research masters for the first time, and cited modelling showing a female science graduate's loan repayment time would rise from 8.4 to 13.9 years under the new bond-rate interest.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, arguing there is no evidence fee deregulation would reduce low socioeconomic student participation, which has stayed around 14.5 per cent despite past fee rises, noted tradespeople currently fund 60 per cent of the cost of a bachelor degree, and said the package requires universities to invest 20 per cent of additional revenue into scholarships for disadvantaged students.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, saying it would disadvantage regional students, and said Charles Darwin University estimates it will lose $50.4 million as a direct result of the cuts, with 75 per cent of its students being mature age learners who would face a mortgage-sized debt to study.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, arguing regional universities like Charles Darwin University, with 7.3 per cent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander enrolment and 63 per cent regional and remote students, would be disadvantaged by a scholarship scheme funded through fee rises, and warned CDU faces a $50.4 million funding cut over the four years from 2016 to 2019.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, defending the government's right to make policy changes without an explicit election mandate, noted $37 billion will fund higher education teaching over the next four years, and cited a straw poll where 70 per cent of James Cook University students did not know their HECS contribution rate.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, accusing the government of breaking its pre-election promise of no cuts to education, and detailing cuts including $5.8 billion from universities, $3.2 billion from HELP and abolition of the $3.5 billion Education Investment Fund, warning of $100,000-plus degrees.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, noting Australian taxpayers currently meet 60 per cent of every university degree's cost, and highlighted that less than 43 per cent of Braddon school leavers complete year 12, arguing expanded diploma and sub-bachelor funding would open alternative education pathways in the electorate.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, highlighting $11 billion over four years for university research, $150 million for the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy, and 100 new Future Fellowships a year, while noting the reforms would create 80,000 additional university places by 2018.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill as a broken election promise, citing a Parliamentary Budget Office finding of a $2.5 billion university funding shortfall within a decade, and projecting engineering degree debts of $98,000 to $113,000 and nursing fees doubling from $25,000 to $50,000 under deregulation.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, arguing the government broke its pre-election 'no cuts to education' promise and its Real Solutions pledge to continue current university funding arrangements, and warned universities cannot guarantee prospective students what fees they will face once deregulation and compounding interest take effect.

Rejected Labor's claims that university fees would double or triple, noting higher education funding rises from $8.97 billion in 2013 to 2014 to $9.465 billion in 2017 to 2018, and cited Group of Eight estimates that free university degrees would cost almost $133 billion over the next 15 years.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that its $5.8 billion funding reduction, fee deregulation, altered HECS interest rate, and research cuts would disadvantage low-income, regional, Tasmanian and female students, including through higher debts and reduced university services.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that expanded Commonwealth funding, scholarships, fee competition and HELP would broaden opportunities, including regionally, while noting a 20 per cent reduction in the Commonwealth Grant Scheme and a maximum interest rate of six per cent.

Argued that fee deregulation and funding cuts would make higher education unaffordable for working-class, regional and mature-age students, threatening regional campuses; opposed the bill as inconsistent with broad access, citing personal and community examples of education transforming opportunity.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014, arguing that competition and deregulation would increase choice and opportunity, including for regional students, while citing $37 billion in funding over the next four financial years.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill 2014, noting $37 billion will go to higher education over the next four years, that students would pay 50 per cent of course costs instead of 40 per cent, and highlighted the University of Tasmania's ranking in the world's top 200 universities for research and diversity.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Amendment Bill, citing nearly $6 billion in cuts including a 20 per cent reduction to the Commonwealth Grant Scheme for teaching, warned degrees could cost more than $100,000, and cited the National Tertiary Education Union, representing about 28,000 staff, in criticizing the lack of consultation with universities.

Continued supporting the higher education reforms, advocated for a $10,000 a year tertiary access allowance to help regional students meet living-away-from-home costs of up to $15,000 a year, and said the reforms would create an extra 80,000 government-subsidised places by 2018, shifting the student share of education costs from about 40 to 50 per cent.

Supported the higher education reforms, noting Australia has eight universities in the world's top 200 compared with China's five, said the reforms include an extra $371 million in Commonwealth support and shift the student cost share from 40 to 50 per cent, and cited research that a university education boosts lifetime earnings by 75 per cent.

Expressed bewilderment at rural and regional government MPs, including the member for Grey and the member for Riverina, defending higher education reforms he argued would harm regional universities and their campuses.

Supported the higher education reforms, arguing they would let regional campuses like Deakin University's Warrnambool campus compete on price and cost of living instead of charging the same fees as its Geelong and Melbourne campuses, and noted education is Australia's fourth-largest export, quoting a 16 April 2012 interview in which former minister Kate Ellis welcomed HECS-style loans for TAFE students.

Opposed the bill, contrasting Labor's increase in higher education funding from $8 billion to $14 billion between 2007 and 2013 with the government's $5.8 billion cut, noted Labor's student start-up scholarships helped 427,000 Australians and relocation scholarships helped 76,000, and detailed a further $3.2 billion cut from changing the HECS-HELP repayment threshold and a $1.1 billion cut to student support places.
